definition: This topic concerns two linked questions: whether a mind or self can be simulated (reproduced well enough to count as real) and whether our minds and world are themselves being simulated or projected by another mind. Dick treats simulation not as counterfeit but as a mode of reality that can equal or surpass the original.
pkd_relevance: Dick repeatedly stages worlds that are projections, hallucinations, or overlays generated by a mind, one's own, another's, or a divine intelligence. The unsettling move is his refusal to treat the simulated as merely fake; a projected world can be more alive than the 'real' one it displaces. Applied to the self, this means a simulated mind might be authentic, and applied to the cosmos, it means reality may be a mind's projection rather than brute matter.
in_the_fiction: *Ubik*, *Eye in the Sky*, and *The Three Stigmata of Palmer Eldritch* build worlds that turn out to be projected from a controlling consciousness, so that characters inhabit another mind's simulation without knowing it. *We Can Build You*'s simulacra raise the parallel question of whether a mind can be built well enough to be a person. Across the fiction, the boundary between a simulated psyche and a genuine one, and between a projected world and a real one, is kept deliberately porous.
in_the_exegesis: The Exegesis makes the projected-world idea metaphysical doctrine: our reality (Form II) is a 'fake' that only exists insofar as it is penetrated and animated by ZEBRA, the projection of Form I, which 'is alive, is here, + imparts life to our universe.' Dick recants his earlier view that such simulation is evil or lesser, concluding it is 'not less than what it simulates but more,' angelic rather than a mere 'simulacra-reflex machine.' Reality is thus a mind (Zebra/VALIS) overlaying and projecting the world, a simulation whose author is divine.
intellectual_background: The theme reaches back to Plato's cave, Descartes's evil demon, Berkeleyan idealism (reality as ideas in a mind), and Gnostic accounts of a demiurgic projection, all of which Dick knew. It also anticipates the modern simulation hypothesis and virtual-reality debates by decades. Dick's distinctive twist is theological: the simulator is not a deceiver to be escaped but potentially a divine mind whose projection redeems an otherwise dead world.
scholarly_debate: Dick is now routinely cited as a precursor to simulation-argument and virtual-reality discourse, and critics debate how far that framing fits a body of work rooted in Gnostic theology rather than computation. A central interpretive dispute is whether the projecting mind is malign (the demiurge's occluding illusion) or benign (Zebra's life-giving overlay), a tension Dick himself never fully resolves and appears to reverse over the course of the Exegesis.
